questions.question: Why is evaluating a generative model harder than evaluating a standard classifier?
options: Because there is no single ground-truth output for each prompt, so quality and prompt adherence must be estimated indirectly
Because generative models cannot produce numeric outputs
Because classifiers never require held-out datasets
Because all generative metrics are exact and architecture-independent
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the evaluation problem around sample quality and conditioning adherence, neither of which has a closed-form answer. Since many different images can be acceptable for one prompt, you need proxy metrics and preference judgments instead of a simple accuracy target.

questions.question: If you only measured text-image similarity for a text-to-image model, what important aspect could you still miss?
options: Whether the generated distribution actually looks realistic or diverse overall
Whether prompts contain nouns
Whether the model used a VAE during training
Whether the GPU batch size was large enough
questions.explanation: A prompt-adherence score can tell you whether images align with their text, but not whether samples are high-quality or match the real image distribution. The lesson therefore separates sample-quality metrics like FID from adherence metrics like CLIP score.

questions.question: What does FID compute according to the lesson?
options: A Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits to real and generated feature distributions in Inception space
The exact pixel-wise MSE between real and generated images
An Elo score from pairwise human votes
The cosine similarity between prompt and image embeddings
questions.explanation: The FID section describes extracting Inception-v3 features, fitting a Gaussian to real and generated pools, and measuring their Fréchet distance. Lower FID means the generated feature distribution is closer to the real one in that feature space.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist on using at least about 10,000 samples when reporting FID?
options: Because FID becomes undefined above 10,000 samples
Because Inception features only exist for datasets of that size
Because small sample sizes underestimate covariance and can produce falsely optimistic FID values
Because CLIP score cannot be computed on smaller runs
questions.explanation: One of the main failure modes listed for FID is small-N bias. With too few samples, covariance estimates are poor and the score can look artificially low, making weak models appear stronger than they are.

questions.question: What evaluation practice does the lesson recommend instead of trusting any single metric alone?
options: Report only the best seed and the lowest FID
Use FID, an adherence metric such as CLIP score or CMMD, blinded preference testing, and qualitative failure analysis together
Replace all human review with GPT-4 judging
Compare models only on prompts they likely saw during training
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly says any single metric is a lie. A credible report combines sample-quality measurement, prompt-adherence measurement, pairwise preference testing, and direct inspection of failure modes so that one metric's blind spots are covered by the others.
